---
title: "Sonic Pi cheat sheet"
---

Here's the working subset of Sonic Pi the book actually uses, arranged by the
musical job each call does. That ordering is deliberate: you'll usually know
what you want to happen to the sound before you remember what the call is
named. For your installed version the built-in help pane is the authority, and
it's normally the fastest place to keep going once you've found the right
neighbourhood.

## Sound

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| `play :c4` | Play a note. Accepts symbols or MIDI integers. |
| `play_chord [:c4, :e4, :g4]` | Play notes together. |
| `sample :bd_haus` | Play a recorded sample. |
| `use_synth :prophet` | Set the instrument for what follows. |
| `synth :pluck, note: :c4` | Play one note on a named synth without switching. |

The pitch starts the event. Everything after it decides how that event occupies
acoustic space, and these are the `play` options you'll reach for most:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `amp: 0.7` | Scale amplitude. Values above 1 are allowed and can clip. |
| `pan: -0.5` | Place the sound left to right, from -1 to 1. |
| `attack: 0.02` | Time taken to reach peak amplitude. |
| `decay: 0.1` | Time taken to fall from the peak to sustain level. |
| `sustain: 0.4` | Time held at the sustain level. |
| `release: 0.6` | Fade time after sustain. |
| `cutoff: 90` | Low-pass filter cutoff, written as a MIDI note number. |

`play` returns a synth node, and `control` changes a node that's already
running. Reach for it when a lesson needs a bend or a fade inside a single note.

```ruby
voice = play :c4, sustain: 2, note_slide: 0.5
sleep 1
control voice, note: :g4
```

## Time

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| `sleep 1` | Advance one beat. |
| `use_bpm 96` | Set the tempo. |
| `live_loop :name do ... end` | A named loop that runs concurrently and can be redefined while running. |
| `in_thread do ... end` | Run a block concurrently, once. |
| `sync :name` / `cue :name` | Wait for, and send, a start signal. |

One beat lasts `60.0 / bpm` seconds. Keep your score durations in beats and a
single tempo change rescales the whole performance without you rewriting one
event.

`at` schedules several offsets from the same starting point:

```ruby
at [0, 0.5, 1.5], [:c4, :e4, :g4] do |note|
  play note
end
sleep 2
```

## Patterns and state

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| `ring(1, 2, 3)` | Build a circular sequence. |
| `pattern.tick` | Advance the current thread's counter and index the ring. |
| `pattern.look` | Read at the current counter without advancing. |
| `tick_reset` | Reset counters in the current thread. |
| `set :name, value` | Store named Sonic Pi state. |
| `get :name` | Read named Sonic Pi state. |

Counters belong to their thread. So two live loops can tick through rings side
by side without stealing positions from each other. When two rings inside one
loop need separate counters, name those counters explicitly in the full Sonic Pi
call.

## Envelope

An envelope describes the life of a synth node: `attack`, `decay`, `sustain`,
and `release`, all measured in beats. `amp` scales its level, and `pan` places
it between -1 on the left and 1 on the right.

Here's the part that catches people out. A note's audible life often runs past
the `sleep` that follows it, because `sleep` moves the score cursor while the
envelope describes the synth node. Long release times overlap later notes, which
is a feature right up until it isn't.

## Music helpers

| Call | Returns |
|---|---|
| `note(:c4)` | `60` |
| `note_info(:c4)` | A structure with name, octave, and MIDI number. |
| `scale(:c4, :major)` | A ring of the scale's notes. |
| `chord(:c4, :major)` | A ring of the chord's notes. |
| `chord_invert(chord(:c4, :major), 1)` | The chord, inverted. |
| `hz_to_midi(440)` / `midi_to_hz(69)` | Convert between frequency and note number. |

Rings from `scale` and `chord` index and iterate like ordinary arrays. Call
`.to_a` when you want a printed comparison to read cleanly.

## Samples

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| `sample :bd_haus` | Trigger a built-in sample. |
| `sample_duration :loop_amen` | Return the sample length in seconds. |
| `sample :loop_amen, beat_stretch: 4` | Stretch a loop to four beats. |
| `sample :ambi_choir, rate: -1` | Play a sample backwards. |

Sample names are symbols. Trust the completion menu or the built-in help over a
name you remember from a different Sonic Pi version, because the libraries move
between releases.

## Randomness

`rrand(lo, hi)` gives you a float, `rrand_i(lo, hi)` an integer, `choose` picks
from a list, and `one_in(n)` gives you a probability. Put `use_random_seed 42`
at the top of any example whose output should be reproducible.

Random calls made in separate threads draw from separate deterministic streams.
Move a random call into another loop and your result changes, even though the
seed didn't.

## Effects

```ruby
with_fx :reverb, room: 0.8 do
  play :c4
end
```

`:reverb`, `:echo`, `:lpf`, `:hpf`, and `:distortion` cover most of the signal
shaping in the lessons. Effects nest, and their order changes the signal path.
Distortion outside reverb distorts a dry note and then puts it in a room. Swap
the blocks and you distort the reverberant tail along with the note.

```ruby
with_fx :distortion, distort: 0.2 do
  with_fx :reverb, room: 0.7 do
    play :e3, release: 2
  end
end
```

## Inspection and failure

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| `puts value` | Print a value in the log. |
| `print value` | Print without adding a line break. |
| `raise "message"` | Stop the current run with an explicit error. |
| `assert condition` | Fail when a Sonic Pi assertion is false. |

When a note disappears, print the score data before you touch the synth. Check
pitch, onset, duration, and amplitude in that order. A zero duration or a zero
amplitude looks exactly like a scheduler bug, while the scheduler is doing
precisely what your event asked it to do.

## Fresh-buffer checklist

A self-contained example should survive amnesia. Press Stop, switch to an unused
buffer, paste the block, run it. Every `define`, variable, synth selection,
tempo, and random seed has to sit above its first use. A clean second run in a
buffer full of remembered definitions proves far less than it looks like it
proves.
